definition: A fuzzy concept is an idea of which the boundaries of application can vary considerably according to context or conditions, instead of being fixed once and for all.
details: That means the idea is somewhat vague or imprecise. Yet it is not unclear or meaningless. It has a definite meaning, which can often be made more exact with further elaboration and specification — including a closer definition of the context in which the concept is used. The inverse of a "fuzzy concept" is a "crisp concept" (i.e. a precise concept). Fuzzy concepts are often used to navigate imprecision in the real world, when precise information is not available and an approximate indication is sufficient to be helpful. Although the linguist George Philip Lakoff already defined the semantics of a fuzzy concept in 1973 (inspired by an unpublished 1971 paper by Eleanor Rosch,) the term "fuzzy concept" rarely received a standalone entry in dictionaries, handbooks and encyclopedias. Sometimes it was defined in encyclopedia articles on fuzzy logic, or it was simply equated with a mathematical “fuzzy set”. A fuzzy concept can be "fuzzy" for many different reasons in different contexts. This makes it harder to provide a precise definition that covers all cases. explainer.lead: Some useful ideas resist a single permanent boundary: what counts in one setting may not count in another. Fuzzy concepts let people communicate and reason with that flexibility while still conveying a definite meaning.

tiers.eli5: Think of the word “tall”: someone who seems tall in a classroom might not seem tall on a basketball team. The word still means something useful, but its boundary moves with the situation. Saying which group you are comparing people with makes your meaning clearer.
tiers.practitioner: In a specification or model, treat a fuzzy concept as a meaningful label whose applicability depends on context. State the domain, conditions, and intended examples before turning it into a crisp working rule; do not assume that it must be represented as a mathematical fuzzy set.
tiers.paperLevel: A fuzzy concept C has a context-dependent extension: its boundary of application varies with context or conditions, unlike a crisp concept with a fixed boundary. George Philip Lakoff defined the semantics of a fuzzy concept in 1973, inspired by Eleanor Rosch’s unpublished 1971 paper. No single precise definition covers every reason for fuzziness, and a fuzzy concept is not simply equivalent to a fuzzy set.

explainer.example: A primary-school teacher and a basketball coach may apply “tall” to different ranges of people. Each use is meaningful, and naming the comparison group makes the intended boundary clearer.

usedIn.name: Fuzzy logic
usedIn.detail: Fuzzy concepts have sometimes been explained within treatments of fuzzy logic, though they are not identical to fuzzy sets.

explainer.intuition: A fuzzy concept is useful without having one fixed edge. Its application can shift with circumstances, while its core meaning remains understandable.
howItWorks: Begin with an idea that has a definite meaning.
Interpret its application within the current context.
Allow its boundaries to vary with relevant conditions.
Add context and specification when greater exactness is needed.
Use an approximate indication when precise information is unavailable.
explainer.whyItMatters: Fuzzy concepts help people handle real-world imprecision when exact information is missing but an approximate indication is still helpful. They also show why adding context can turn an apparently vague statement into a more precise one.
misconceptions: Fuzzy does not mean unclear or meaningless.
A fuzzy concept is not simply a mathematical fuzzy set.
Its meaning can often be sharpened with further specification.
